source: Work Along a Path
W = ∫F · dr adds up only the part of the force along each small step of the path.
Students multiply the size of the force by the path length, ignoring the angle between them.

Work by a Variable Force handled motion along a straight line with the force along that line. Now let the path curve and the force point any way. The tool is The Dot Product and the Angle Between Vectors: it keeps only the part of the force along each little step.

$$W = \int_{\text{path}} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \int \left(F_x\,dx + F_y\,dy + F_z\,dz\right).$$ Only the component of $\vec{F}$ along the direction of motion does work. For a straight path and a constant force, $W = \vec{F}\cdot\Delta\vec{r} = F\,d\cos\theta$.

Break the path into tiny straight steps $d\vec{r}$. On one step the force is nearly constant, and the work is $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = F\,dr\cos\theta$: a force perpendicular to the step ($\theta = 90^\circ$) does nothing, a force along it does the most. Add up the steps and you have a line integral. To compute it, describe the path with one parameter, such as $x$ or $t$, and write $dx$, $dy$ and the force in terms of it.
The field $\vec{F} = \langle y, 2x \rangle$ along $y = x^2$. Arrows show the force; the running total is $\int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$.
You pull a sled $10\ \text{m}$ across level snow with a $40\ \text{N}$ rope tension at $30^\circ$ above horizontal. How much work does the rope do?
Pulling a sled
$W = Fd\cos\theta = 40(10)\cos 30^\circ$.
The vertical part, $40\sin 30^\circ = 20\ \text{N}$, lightens the sled but does no work.
Find the work done by $\vec{F} = \langle y, 2x \rangle$ (N, m) on a particle moving along $y = x^2$ from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$.
A field along a curve
$\tfrac{5}{3}\ \text{J}$ (and $1.5\ \text{J}$ along the straight line).
On the path $y = x^2$ and $dy = 2x\,dx$.
$W = \int_0^1 5x^2\,dx = \tfrac{5}{3} \approx 1.67\ \text{J}$.
Along the straight line $y = x$ instead: $\int_0^1 (x + 2x)\,dx = 1.5\ \text{J}$. A different path, a different work.

Multiplying the size of the force by the length of the path. For the sled that gives $400\ \text{J}$ instead of $346\ \text{J}$. It ignores the angle: the upward part of the pull never moves the sled forward. Check: if the force were straight up, the formula $Fd$ would still give 400 J, though the sled wouldn't budge forward at all. The dot product gives zero, as it should.
The work depended on the path in the second example. Forces for which it never does are special and very useful; they are the subject of Conservative Forces.
